lessons.title: Newborn calf care: colostrum management and navel dipping
lessons.body:
The first hours of a calf's life determine whether it will thrive or struggle. As soon as a calf is born, ensure it breathes and clear mucus from its nose and mouth. The single most important step is feeding colostrumâthe first milk from the motherâwithin the first 2 hours of birth. A newborn calf's gut can only absorb antibodies for about 6 hours, so timing is critical. Give 2 to 3 litres of clean, high-quality colostrum using a clean bottle and teat or an oesophageal feeder. If the dam cannot be milked, use frozen colostrum from a healthy cow, thawed in warm water (never boiling). Test colostrum quality with a colostrometer; good colostrum has a reading above 50 mg/ml IgG. If you don't have a colostrometer, thick, creamy yellow colostrum is usually good. Feed colostrum again 12 hours later, another 2 litres. 

Navel dipping prevents infection. Mix 7% iodine or chlorhexidine solution in a small cup. Dip the entire navel stump for 5 seconds, ensuring full coverage. Do this immediately after birth and again 6 hours later. If the navel is bleeding, tie it with clean thread. Keep the calf in a clean, dry, well-bedded pen away from adult cows to reduce disease risk. 

In many African settings, calves are left with the dam, but this risks poor colostrum intake if the dam rejects the calf or if the calf is weak. Instead, restrain the cow and assist the calf to suckle or milk the cow by hand. If the calf is weak, use a stomach tube. Always record the calf's birth date, dam, and colostrum feeding times. 

After the first 24 hours, continue feeding transition milk (the milk from the next 2-3 milkings) as it still contains some antibodies and nutrients. Provide fresh, clean water at all times. By day 2, the calf should be active and alert. If it is dull, scouring, or not suckling, consult a vet immediately. Good newborn care reduces calf mortality from 20% to under 5%.

lessons.title: Feeding programs for calves: milk replacer and starter feed
lessons.body:
From day 2 to weaning, calves need a consistent feeding program. If the dam is milked for sale, use milk replacer. Mix 125 grams of milk replacer powder per litre of clean warm water (about 40Â°C). Feed 4 to 6 litres per day, split into two feedings (morning and evening). Use a clean bucket or bottle with a teat. Never feed more than 2.5 litres at one time to avoid digestive upset. If using whole milk, feed 10% of the calf's body weight dailyâa 40 kg calf gets 4 litres. 

Start offering calf starter feed from day 3. Use a shallow trough and place a small handful of fresh, coarse starter (18-20% protein) in it. Calves will nibble at it. By 2 weeks, they may eat 100-200 grams per day. By 8 weeks, they should eat 1-1.5 kg per day. Starter feed should be palatable: mix in a little molasses or ground maize if needed. Always provide fresh, clean waterâcalves drink water even when on milk. 

Introduce good-quality hay from week 2. Fine-stemmed hay or chopped forage helps rumen development. Avoid dusty or mouldy hay. In Africa, use locally available feeds like lucerne, desmodium, or sweet potato vines, but ensure they are wilted, not wet. 

Feeding schedule: Week 1-2: colostrum then milk replacer or whole milk, 4-6 L/day. Week 3-4: same milk, plus starter and hay. Week 5-6: reduce milk to 2-3 L/day, increase starter to 1 kg. Week 7-8: milk once a day, starter 1.5 kg. By week 8-10, wean if the calf eats 1.5 kg starter daily. 

Always wash feeding equipment with hot water and disinfectant after each use. Dirty equipment causes scours. Keep records of milk and feed intake. If a calf refuses milk, check for fever or scours. Adjust feed graduallyâsudden changes cause diarrhoea. In hot weather, feed early morning and late evening to reduce stress.

lessons.title: Housing and environment for calves
lessons.body:
Calves need a dry, draught-free, well-ventilated space. In Africa, many farmers use individual pens or hutches. A calf hutch made from local materialsâwood, thatch, or corrugated ironâshould be at least 1.2 m wide, 1.5 m deep, and 1.2 m high. Place it on a slight slope so water drains away. The floor should be earth or concrete, covered with 10-15 cm of dry straw or wood shavings. Never use wet or muddy beddingâit causes navel infections and pneumonia. 

Ventilation is critical but avoid direct draughts. In hot climates, orient the hutch so the opening faces away from prevailing winds but allows cross-flow of air. In cold or rainy seasons, use a removable canvas or plastic sheet to block wind and rain. The temperature inside should not exceed 30Â°C; if it does, provide shade with a tree or shade cloth. 

Keep calves separated from adult cows. A distance of at least 5 metres prevents disease transmission. If group housing, limit to 4-6 calves of similar age, with 2.5 square metres per calf. Provide a clean, dry lying area and a separate feeding area. 

Clean the pen daily: remove wet bedding and manure. Disinfect weekly with a 2% caustic soda solution or commercial disinfectant. Allow the pen to dry in the sun. Provide fresh water in a clean bucket, and feed from a trough that calves cannot step in. 

In free-range systems, ensure calves have access to a shaded, dry resting area. Rotate pens to prevent build-up of parasites. Always check for predators (dogs, wild animals) and secure the area with a fence. A well-designed calf house reduces respiratory disease and scours, the two biggest killers of young stock.

lessons.title: Weaning strategies and transition to group housing
lessons.body:
Weaning is the most stressful period in a calf's life. The goal is to move from liquid milk to solid feed without weight loss or disease. Start planning at 6 weeks: reduce milk gradually. For example, if feeding 4 L/day, drop to 3 L for 3 days, then 2 L for 3 days, then 1 L for 3 days, then stop. Meanwhile, increase starter feed to 1.5-2 kg per day. By 8-10 weeks, a calf eating 1.5 kg of starter and 0.5 kg of hay daily is ready to wean. 

Wean based on feed intake, not age. A calf should weigh at least 70-80 kg (double birth weight) and have a rumen developed enough to digest forage. If a calf is not eating enough starter, delay weaning by one week. 

After weaning, move calves to group housing. Groups of 4-8 calves of similar size and age work best. Provide 2.5-3 square metres per calf in a well-bedded pen with access to a dry outdoor area. Introduce calves to the group early in the morning when they are hungry, so they focus on feed rather than fighting. Monitor for bullyingâsmaller calves may not get enough feed. Use multiple feeding spaces (one trough space per calf) and water points. 

Transition diet: continue the same starter feed for 2 weeks after weaning. Then gradually introduce a grower ration (16% protein) and good-quality forage. Increase forage slowly to avoid bloat. 

Keep stress low: avoid dehorning, castration, or vaccination during the first week after weaning. Provide clean water and shade. Weigh calves monthly to track growth. If a calf loses weight, isolate it and check for parasites or disease. Successful weaning sets the stage for healthy heifer growth.

lessons.title: Heifer growth and development targets
lessons.body:
A dairy heifer must reach key weight and height targets to calve at 24 months and produce milk profitably. Weigh your heifers monthly using a weigh tape or scale. Record weights in a notebook. The targets: birth weight 30-40 kg; weaning (8-10 weeks) 70-80 kg; 6 months 140-160 kg; 12 months 220-250 kg; 15 months (breeding age) 280-320 kg; 24 months (calving) 400-450 kg. 

Height at withers is also important. At 12 months, a heifer should be 110-115 cm tall; at 15 months, 120-125 cm. Use a measuring stick or a marked wall. If a heifer is below target, increase feed quality and quantity. If above, reduce energy to avoid fat deposition in the udder. 

Feed to target: from 3 to 6 months, feed 2-3 kg of grower ration (16% protein) plus free-choice forage. From 6 to 12 months, feed 1-2 kg concentrate plus good pasture or hay. From 12 to 24 months, feed 1-2 kg concentrate and forage, adjusting based on body condition. Provide mineral licks. 

In Africa, use locally available feeds: maize silage, Napier grass, lucerne, cottonseed cake, molasses. For protein, use sunflower cake or fish meal if available. Always provide clean waterâa heifer drinks 20-40 litres per day. 

Monitor body condition score (BCS) monthly: aim for 3.0-3.5 (on a 1-5 scale) at breeding and 3.5 at calving. Too thin (BCS <2.5) delays puberty; too fat (BCS >4) causes calving problems. 

Health checks: deworm every 3 months, vaccinate against brucellosis and anthrax as per local schedule. Hoof trimming twice a year. If a heifer fails to reach 280 kg by 15 months, consult an extension officer. Proper heifer rearing reduces age at first calving and increases lifetime milk yield.

lessons.title: Health management for young stock
lessons.body:
Young stock health is about prevention, not just treatment. The main diseases are scours (diarrhoea), pneumonia, and parasites. Scours kills quicklyâwithin 24 hours. Causes include dirty feeding equipment, overfeeding, or E. coli. Signs: watery faeces, sunken eyes, weakness. Treat with oral rehydration solution (1 litre water + 1 teaspoon salt + 6 teaspoons sugar) and continue milk feeding. If severe, use antibiotics prescribed by a vet. 

Pneumonia causes coughing, rapid breathing, and fever. It spreads in poorly ventilated, damp pens. Prevent by good ventilation, dry bedding, and avoiding overcrowding. Vaccinate against pneumonia if available. Treat early with antibioticsâwaiting reduces lung function permanently. 

Parasites: internal worms cause weight loss and diarrhoea. Deworm calves at 2 months, then every 3 months. Use albendazole or ivermectin as per vet advice. External parasites (ticks, lice) cause anaemia. Spray or dip calves with acaricide every 2 weeks in tick-prone areas. 

Vaccination schedule: at 2 weeks, vaccinate against blackleg and malignant oedema (if in endemic area). At 1 month, vaccinate against anthrax and botulism. At 3 months, vaccinate against brucellosis (heifers only). At 6 months, booster. Always follow local veterinary recommendations. 

Daily observation: check each calf for appetite, alertness, and manure consistency. A healthy calf is curious, eats well, and has firm droppings. Isolate sick calves immediately. Keep a health record for each calf: date, symptoms, treatment, and outcome. 

Biosecurity: limit visitors, disinfect boots and equipment, quarantine new animals for 2 weeks. Provide clean water and feed. In Africa, many diseases are preventable with simple hygiene and timely vaccination. If you see blood in manure or sudden death, call a vet immediatelyâit could be coccidiosis or anthrax.

quiz.q: What is the most critical time to feed colostrum to a newborn calf?
quiz.explanation: A calf's gut can only absorb antibodies for about 6 hours, so feeding within 2 hours is essential.

quiz.q: How much colostrum should a newborn calf receive in the first feeding?
quiz.explanation: A calf needs 2-3 litres of colostrum in the first feeding to get enough antibodies.

quiz.q: What solution is recommended for navel dipping?
quiz.explanation: 7% iodine is a standard disinfectant for navel dipping to prevent infection.

quiz.q: How many times should navel dipping be done?
options: B) Twice: at birth and 6 hours later
C) Three times daily for a week
D) Only if the navel bleeds
quiz.explanation: Dipping at birth and again after 6 hours ensures thorough disinfection.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mixing rate for milk replacer?
options: A) 125 g powder per litre of water
quiz.explanation: 125 g per litre is the standard concentration for milk replacer.

quiz.q: At what age should calves start eating starter feed?
quiz.explanation: Calves can be introduced to starter feed from day 3 to encourage rumen development.

quiz.q: How much starter feed should a calf eat by 8 weeks to be ready for weaning?
quiz.explanation: A calf eating 1.5 kg of starter daily is ready to be weaned.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for mixing milk replacer?
quiz.explanation: Mixing at 40Â°C ensures the powder dissolves well without destroying nutrients.

quiz.q: Why should feeding equipment be washed after each use?
quiz.explanation: Dirty equipment harbours bacteria that cause scours in calves.

quiz.q: What is the minimum floor area recommended for a calf hutch?
quiz.explanation: A hutch of 1.2 m wide by 1.5 m deep gives the calf enough space to move and lie down.

quiz.q: What type of bedding is best for calf pens?
options: B) Dry straw or wood shavings
quiz.explanation: Dry straw or wood shavings absorb moisture and keep the calf clean and dry.

quiz.q: How often should calf pens be disinfected?
quiz.explanation: Weekly disinfection with a 2% caustic soda solution helps prevent disease build-up.

quiz.q: What is the recommended group size for group housing of calves?
quiz.explanation: Groups of 4-8 calves of similar age reduce competition and stress.

quiz.q: How should weaning be done?
options: B) Reduce milk gradually over 1-2 weeks
quiz.explanation: Gradual reduction of milk allows the calf to adjust and prevents weight loss.

quiz.q: What is a key indicator that a calf is ready to wean?
options: B) It eats 1.5 kg of starter daily
quiz.explanation: Feed intake, not age, is the best indicator of weaning readiness.

quiz.q: What should be provided during the transition to group housing?
options: A) One feeding space for all
B) Multiple feeding and water points
quiz.explanation: Multiple feeding spaces ensure all calves get enough feed and reduce bullying.

quiz.q: What is the target weight for a heifer at 12 months of age?
quiz.explanation: A well-grown heifer should weigh 220-250 kg at 12 months.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height at withers for a 15-month-old heifer?
quiz.explanation: Height of 120-125 cm at 15 months indicates proper skeletal growth.

quiz.q: What body condition score (BCS) should a heifer have at breeding?
quiz.explanation: BCS 3.0-3.5 is ideal for breeding; too thin or too fat reduces fertility.

quiz.q: How often should heifers be dewormed?
quiz.explanation: Deworming every 3 months controls internal parasites and supports growth.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of scours in a calf?
quiz.explanation: Watery faeces is the primary sign of scours, which can quickly dehydrate a calf.

quiz.q: What is the correct oral rehydration solution for a scouring calf?
options: A) 1 L water + 1 tsp salt + 6 tsp sugar
quiz.explanation: This mixture replaces lost electrolytes and fluids effectively.

quiz.q: What disease causes coughing and rapid breathing in calves?
quiz.explanation: Pneumonia affects the lungs and causes respiratory distress.

quiz.q: How can pneumonia be prevented in calf pens?
options: B) Good ventilation and dry bedding
quiz.explanation: Fresh air and dryness reduce the build-up of pathogens that cause pneumonia.

quiz.q: Why should sick calves be isolated?
quiz.explanation: Isolation stops contagious diseases from spreading to healthy calves.

quiz.q: What is a common external parasite of calves?
quiz.explanation: Ticks attach to the skin and can transmit diseases and cause anaemia.

quiz.q: How often should calves be vaccinated against brucellosis?
quiz.explanation: Brucellosis vaccination is typically given to heifers at 3-6 months of age.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a healthy calf?
quiz.explanation: A healthy calf is alert, has a good appetite, and firm droppings.

quiz.q: What is the target age at first calving for a dairy heifer?
quiz.explanation: Calving at 24 months reduces rearing costs and increases lifetime productivity.

quiz.q: What should you do if a heifer fails to reach 280 kg by 15 months?
quiz.explanation: An extension officer can help identify nutritional or health problems and adjust the feeding program.
